claim: Jyvaskylavirus is the first giant virus isolated from Finland.
source: Here, we describe Jyvaskylavirus, the first giant virus isolated from Finland.
evidence: Stated directly in the abstract and introduction sections of the manuscript.

claim: Jyvaskylavirus is a clade B marseillevirus.
source: This clade B marseillevirus was found in Acanthamoeba castellanii from a composting soil sample in Jyväskylä, Central Finland.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis and genome comparison data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Jyvaskylavirus was isolated from Acanthamoeba castellanii from a composting soil sample in Jyväskylä, Central Finland.
source: This clade B marseillevirus was found in Acanthamoeba castellanii from a composting soil sample in Jyväskylä, Central Finland.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract and supported by methods section describing sample collection and isolation.

claim: The Jyvaskylavirus virion was reconstructed to 6.3 Å resolution using cryo-electron microscopy.
source: We reconstructed the Jyvaskylavirus particle to 6.3 Å resolution using cryo-electron microscopy.
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM data collection and reconstruction methods described in the manuscript.

claim: The Jyvaskylavirus virion has a diameter of approximately 2500 Å.
source: The ~2500 Å diameter virion displays structural similarities to other Marseilleviridae giant viruses.
evidence: Measured from cryo-EM reconstruction data.

claim: The Jyvaskylavirus capsid comprises 9240 copies of the major capsid protein.
source: The capsid comprises of 9240 copies of the major capsid protein, encoded by open reading frame (ORF) 184, which possesses a double jellyroll fold arranged in trimers forming pseudo-hexameric capsomers.
evidence: Calculated from structural analysis of the cryo-EM reconstruction.

claim: The major capsid protein of Jyvaskylavirus is encoded by ORF184.
source: The capsid comprises of 9240 copies of the major capsid protein, encoded by open reading frame (ORF) 184, which possesses a double jellyroll fold arranged in trimers forming pseudo-hexameric capsomers.
evidence: Identified through genome annotation and structural modeling using AlphaFold3.

claim: The major capsid protein of Jyvaskylavirus possesses a double jellyroll fold.
source: The capsid comprises of 9240 copies of the major capsid protein, encoded by open reading frame (ORF) 184, which possesses a double jellyroll fold arranged in trimers forming pseudo-hexameric capsomers.
evidence: Determined through AlphaFold3 prediction and fitting into cryo-EM density.

claim: The major capsid protein of Jyvaskylavirus is arranged in trimers forming pseudo-hexameric capsomers.
source: The capsid comprises of 9240 copies of the major capsid protein, encoded by open reading frame (ORF) 184, which possesses a double jellyroll fold arranged in trimers forming pseudo-hexameric capsomers.
evidence: Observed in cryo-EM density and confirmed by structural analysis.

claim: An internal membrane vesicle encloses the genome below the capsid shell in Jyvaskylavirus.
source: Below the capsid shell, the internal membrane vesicle encloses the genome.
evidence: Observed in cryo-EM reconstruction and TEM images.

claim: ORF142 is the penton protein of Jyvaskylavirus.
source: Through cross-structural and -sequence comparisons with other Marseilleviridae using AI-based software in model building and prediction, we elucidated ORF142 as the penton protein, which plugs the 12 vertices of the capsid.
evidence: Identified through cross-structural comparison with Melbournevirus and AlphaFold3 prediction.

claim: The penton protein plugs the 12 vertices of the Jyvaskylavirus capsid.
source: Through cross-structural and -sequence comparisons with other Marseilleviridae using AI-based software in model building and prediction, we elucidated ORF142 as the penton protein, which plugs the 12 vertices of the capsid.
evidence: Determined from structural analysis and fitting into cryo-EM density.

claim: Five additional ORFs were identified in Jyvaskylavirus with models predicted and fitted into densities.
source: Five additional ORFs were identified, with models predicted and fitted into densities that either cap the capsomers externally or stabilize them internally.
evidence: Identified through cross-structural comparison and AlphaFold3 prediction.

claim: Giant viruses were evading discovery for three main reasons: their large size traps them in filters commonly used in virological works, their structure and size makes them visible by Gram staining, and their protist hosts are not as well studied as other host species.
source: Hidden in plain sight for over a century of microbiology research, APMV and other giant viruses were evading discovery for three main reasons: their large size traps them in filters commonly used in virological works, their structure and size makes them visible by Gram staining, and their protist hosts are not as well studied as other host species (Colson et al., 2017; Queiroz et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Giant viruses are included in the nucleo-cytoplasmic large DNA viruses (NCLDVs) group based on common features of their double-stranded DNA genomes, similarity in a few core genes, relative independence of host transcription machinery, partial or complete cytoplasmic replication and formation of viral factories.
source: Common features of their double-stranded DNA genomes, similarity in a few core genes, relative independence of host transcription machinery, partial or complete cytoplasmic replication and formation of viral factories include giant viruses in the nucleo-cytoplasmic large DNA viruses (NCLDVs) group (Iyer et al., 2001; Boyer et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The International Committee of Taxonomy of Viruses (ICTV) classified giant viruses as members of the phylum Nucleocytoviricota of the kingdom Bamfordvirae in the realm Varidnaviria.
source: Recently, the International Committee of Taxonomy of Viruses (ICTV) classified giant viruses as members of the phylum Nucleocytoviricota of the kingdom Bamfordvirae in the realm Varidnaviria (Walker et al., 2019; Simmonds et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to ICTV classification publications.

claim: Giant viruses are ubiquitous in the environment.
source: Isolation efforts and metagenomic data in the last two decades have revealed that giant viruses are ubiquitous in the environment (Moniruzzaman et al., 2020; Schulz et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to metagenomic studies.

claim: Giant virus particles or their DNA have been found from the Antarctica to the Siberian permafrost, in deep-sea sediments and many other sources including urban environments and diverse sample types.
source: Giant virus particles or their DNA have been found from the Antarctica to the Siberian permafrost, in deep-sea sediments and many other sources including urban environments and diverse sample types (Andrade et al., 2018; Legendre et al., 2015; Bäckström et al., 2019; Colson et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous isolation and metagenomic studies.

claim: Jyvaskylavirus genome contains 359,967 base pairs.
source: Jyvaskylavirus contains a 359,967 base pairs (bp) genome, with a 42.80% GC content and 388 predicted open reading frames (ORFs) coding for proteins with sizes that vary between 99 and 1525 amino acids.
evidence: Determined from genome sequencing and assembly.

claim: Jyvaskylavirus genome has a 42.80% GC content.
source: Jyvaskylavirus contains a 359,967 base pairs (bp) genome, with a 42.80% GC content and 388 predicted open reading frames (ORFs) coding for proteins with sizes that vary between 99 and 1525 amino acids.
evidence: Calculated from genome sequence data.

claim: Jyvaskylavirus genome has 388 predicted open reading frames (ORFs).
source: Jyvaskylavirus contains a 359,967 base pairs (bp) genome, with a 42.80% GC content and 388 predicted open reading frames (ORFs) coding for proteins with sizes that vary between 99 and 1525 amino acids.
evidence: Determined through genome annotation using GeneMarkS.

claim: Jyvaskylavirus ORFs code for proteins with sizes that vary between 99 and 1525 amino acids.
source: Jyvaskylavirus contains a 359,967 base pairs (bp) genome, with a 42.80% GC content and 388 predicted open reading frames (ORFs) coding for proteins with sizes that vary between 99 and 1525 amino acids.
evidence: Determined from ORF prediction and annotation.

claim: The positive DNA strand of Jyvaskylavirus codes for 186 ORFs.
source: The positive DNA strand codes for 186 ORFs whereas the other 202 are in the negative strand (Figure 2A; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Determined from genome annotation.

claim: The negative DNA strand of Jyvaskylavirus codes for 202 ORFs.
source: The positive DNA strand codes for 186 ORFs whereas the other 202 are in the negative strand (Figure 2A; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Determined from genome annotation.

claim: Jyvaskylavirus contains DNA polymerase family B encoded by ORF177.
source: During genome annotation, some of the Nucleocytoviricota conserved proteins were detected, including the DNA polymerase family B (ORF177) and the A32-like packaging ATPase (ORF23).
evidence: Identified through genome annotation and sequence homology.

claim: Jyvaskylavirus contains A32-like packaging ATPase encoded by ORF23.
source: During genome annotation, some of the Nucleocytoviricota conserved proteins were detected, including the DNA polymerase family B (ORF177) and the A32-like packaging ATPase (ORF23).
evidence: Identified through genome annotation and sequence homology.

claim: About 67% of Jyvaskylavirus genes code for uncharacterized proteins.
source: The most of Jyvaskylavirus genes (about 67%) code for uncharacterized proteins.
evidence: Calculated from genome annotation results.

claim: Jyvaskylavirus genome contains three histone-like proteins encoded by ORF215, 216, and 320.
source: The second major function category is the DNA replication, recombination, and repair genes, including three histone-like proteins (ORF215, 216, 320), a typical marseillevirus genome feature (Figure 2B; Bryson et al., 2022).
evidence: Identified through genome annotation and comparison with other marseilleviruses.

claim: Three histone-like proteins is a typical marseillevirus genome feature.
source: The second major function category is the DNA replication, recombination, and repair genes, including three histone-like proteins (ORF215, 216, 320), a typical marseillevirus genome feature (Figure 2B; Bryson et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature on marseilleviruses.

claim: Three new ORFans were detected in Jyvaskylavirus: ORF264, 265, and 289.
source: Three new ORFans were detected (ORF264, 265, 289), representing genes that have no significant similarity with any other sequences from the database used in this analysis.
evidence: Determined through BLASTp searches against sequence databases.

claim: ORF264, 265, and 289 represent genes that have no significant similarity with any other sequences from the database used in this analysis.
source: Three new ORFans were detected (ORF264, 265, 289), representing genes that have no significant similarity with any other sequences from the database used in this analysis.
evidence: Determined through BLASTp searches.

claim: ORF264 codes for a putative protein with 108 amino acids.
source: ORF264, 265, and 289 codes for putative proteins with 108, 157, and 119 amino acids, respectively.
evidence: Determined from ORF prediction.

claim: ORF265 codes for a putative protein with 157 amino acids.
source: ORF264, 265, and 289 codes for putative proteins with 108, 157, and 119 amino acids, respectively.
evidence: Determined from ORF prediction.

claim: ORF289 codes for a putative protein with 119 amino acids.
source: ORF264, 265, and 289 codes for putative proteins with 108, 157, and 119 amino acids, respectively.
evidence: Determined from ORF prediction.

claim: Jyvaskylavirus contains three translation factors: a translation initiation factor (ORF154), an elongation factor (ORF318), and a peptide chain release factor (ORF28).
source: We searched for translation-related genes and found three translation factors, including a translation initiation factor (ORF154), an elongation factor (ORF318), and a peptide chain release factor (ORF28).
evidence: Identified through genome annotation and sequence homology.

claim: No tRNAs or aminoacyl tRNA synthetases genes were found in Jyvaskylavirus.
source: No tRNAs or aminoacyl tRNA synthetases genes were found.
evidence: Determined through genome annotation using ARAGORN and other tools.

claim: Most of the BLASTp best hits for Jyvaskylavirus amino acid sequences matched Lausannevirus or Port-miou virus.
source: Furthermore, most of the BLASTp best hits for Jyvaskylavirus amino acid sequences matched Lausannevirus or Port-miou virus that are phylogenetically related to marseilleiviruses from lineage B.
evidence: Determined through BLASTp analysis.

claim: Lausannevirus and Port-miou virus are phylogenetically related to marseilleviruses from lineage B.
source: Furthermore, most of the BLASTp best hits for Jyvaskylavirus amino acid sequences matched Lausannevirus or Port-miou virus that are phylogenetically related to marseilleiviruses from lineage B.
evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Phylogeny based on DNA polymerase family B clusters Jyvaskylavirus within Marseilleviridae family, together with other marseilleviruses from clade B.
source: This observation can also be reinforced by the phylogeny based on DNA polymerase family B, which clusters the Jyvaskylavirus within Marseilleviridae family, together with other marseilleviruses from clade B (Figure 2C, Appendix 1—figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic tree construction and analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Jyvaskylavirus presents genome synteny similarity blocks comparable to those from clade B marseilleviruses.
source: When analyzing the genome synteny of different marseilleviruses genomes, it is shown that Jyvaskylavirus presents similarity blocks comparable to those from clade B marseilleviruses (Appendix 1—figure 3B).
evidence: Determined through synteny analysis using MAUVE program.

claim: Searching the Jyvaskylavirus MCP and DNA polymerase sequences in the MGnify database yields multiple hits with significantly low E-values (<1e-80).
source: Searching the Jyvaskylavirus MCP and DNA polymerase sequences in the MGnify database (Richardson et al., 2023) yields multiple hits with significantly low E-values (<1e-80), as expected from the apparent ubiquity of marseilleviruses.
evidence: Determined through database searches.

claim: Similar sequences to Jyvaskylavirus MCP and DNA polymerase were detected in metagenomes and transcriptomes obtained from drinking water distribution systems of ground and surface waterworks in Central and Eastern Finland.
source: Of note was the detection of similar sequences in metagenomes and transcriptomes obtained from drinking water distribution systems of ground and surface waterworks in Central and Eastern Finland, evidencing that marseilleviruses are prevalent but still unexplored in this region (Tiwari et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to metagenomic study.

claim: Marseilleviruses are prevalent but still unexplored in Central and Eastern Finland.
source: Of note was the detection of similar sequences in metagenomes and transcriptomes obtained from drinking water distribution systems of ground and surface waterworks in Central and Eastern Finland, evidencing that marseilleviruses are prevalent but still unexplored in this region (Tiwari et al., 2021).
evidence: Inferred from metagenomic data showing presence of marseillevirus sequences.

claim: A. castellanii cells appear as mainly oval-shaped with spined structures (acanthopodia) protruding from the cell surface by HIM imaging.
source: By HIM imaging A. castellanii cells appear as mainly oval-shaped with spined structures (acanthopodia) protruding from the cell surface; furthermore, a cell with an elongated shape was captured likely in the process of cell division (Figure 3A).
evidence: Observed in helium ion microscopy images shown in Figure 3A.

claim: One strategy for marseillevirus entry is the triggering of an endosomal-stimulated pathway.
source: One of strategies for marseillevirus entry is the triggering of an endosomal-stimulated pathway (Arantes et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Virions were captured attached to cell regions showing invaginations of the cell membrane, probably indicating the process of endocytosis.
source: We captured a cell with virions attached in regions showing invaginations of the cell membrane, probably indicating the process of endocytosis (Figure 3C).
evidence: Observed in HIM images and inferred from known marseillevirus entry mechanisms.

claim: Extracellular vesicles larger than 500 nm in size containing multiple virions inside were visualized close to burst cells.
source: Extracellular vesicles larger than 500 nm in size containing multiple virions inside were visualized close to burst cells (Figure 3D, left inset).
evidence: Observed in HIM images shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Virion clusters are important for marseilleviruses to reach the required threshold for triggering amoebal phagocytosis.
source: These virion clusters are important for marseilleviruses, which are smaller than other giant viruses, to reach the required threshold for triggering amoebal phagocytosis and thus initiating their infection cycle through this entry mechanism (Arantes et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature on marseillevirus entry mechanisms.

claim: At 24 hpi, Jyvaskylavirus-infected cells are overtaken by virus production, with intracellular vesicles of varying dimensions (e.g. 1–2 µm), which contain already apparent virions.
source: At 24 hpi, the cells are overtaken by virus production, with intracellular vesicles of varying dimensions (e.g. 1–2 µm), which contain already apparent virions (Figure 4A).
evidence: Observed in TEM images of infected cells shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Large viral factories are observed in Jyvaskylavirus-infected cells, with some occupying almost the entire cell area.
source: Large viral factories are observed, with some occupying almost the entire cell area (Figure 4B).
evidence: Observed in TEM images shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Jyvaskylavirus has a triangulation number T=309 (h=7, k=13).
source: Jyvaskylavirus icosahedral virion, determined to 6.3 Å resolution as judged by the gold-standard Fourier shell correlation, possesses a diameter of 2516 Å (vertex-to-vertex) and a triangulation number T=309 (h=7, k=13) (Figure 5A, Appendix 1—figure 4, and Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: Calculated from cryo-EM reconstruction.

claim: The Jyvaskylavirus protein capsid shell is approximately 120 Å thick.
source: The protein capsid shell, approximately 120 Å thick, can be geometrically represented by trisymmetrons and pentasymmetrons as similarly done with other NCLDVs (Figure 5B; Sinkovits and Baker, 2010).
evidence: Measured from cryo-EM reconstruction.

claim: The Jyvaskylavirus trisymmetron comprises 136 pseudo-hexameric capsomers.
source: The trisymmetron and pentasymmetron comprises 136 and 30 pseudo-hexameric capsomers, respectively, along with one penton complex, containing five copies of the penton protein (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Calculated from structural analysis of cryo-EM reconstruction.

claim: The Jyvaskylavirus pentasymmetron comprises 30 pseudo-hexameric capsomers.
source: The trisymmetron and pentasymmetron comprises 136 and 30 pseudo-hexameric capsomers, respectively, along with one penton complex, containing five copies of the penton protein (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Calculated from structural analysis of cryo-EM reconstruction.

claim: The penton complex contains five copies of the penton protein.
source: The trisymmetron and pentasymmetron comprises 136 and 30 pseudo-hexameric capsomers, respectively, along with one penton complex, containing five copies of the penton protein (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Determined from structural analysis.

claim: Jyvaskylavirus icosahedral asymmetric unit (IAU) is composed of 51 pseudo-hexameric capsomers plus 1/3 of the capsomer sitting on the icosahedral threefold axis.
source: Jyvaskylavirus icosahedral asymmetric unit (IAU) is composed of 51 pseudo-hexameric capsomers plus 1/3 of the capsomer sitting on the icosahedral threefold axis (Figure 5C).
evidence: Calculated from structural analysis of cryo-EM reconstruction.

claim: Both the capsid organization and virion size of Jyvaskylavirus are similar to those of other marseilleviruses, such as Melbournevirus and Tokyovirus.
source: Both the capsid organization and virion size are similar to those of other marseilleviruses, such as Melbournevirus and Tokyovirus.
evidence: Based on comparison of structural features.

claim: Pacmanvirus has the same T number (309) and a comparable diameter to Jyvaskylavirus.
source: Pacmanvirus, considered to be at the crossroads between Asfarviridae and Faustoviruses, also possesses the same T number (309) and a comparable diameter to Jyvaskylavirus.
evidence: Based on comparison with published structural data.

claim: ASFV has a T number of 277 and a diameter of approximately 2100 Å.
source: In contrast, other giant viruses, such as ASFV, representative of the Asfarviridae family, have a T number of 277 and a diameter of approximately 2100 Å, while PBCV-1, a member of the Phycodnaviridae family, has a T number of 169 and an average diameter of 1900 Å.
evidence: Based on published structural data.

claim: PBCV-1 has a T number of 169 and an average diameter of 1900 Å.
source: In contrast, other giant viruses, such as ASFV, representative of the Asfarviridae family, have a T number of 277 and a diameter of approximately 2100 Å, while PBCV-1, a member of the Phycodnaviridae family, has a T number of 169 and an average diameter of 1900 Å.
evidence: Based on published structural data.

claim: All of the mentioned viruses (ASFV, PBCV-1, Melbournevirus, Tokyovirus, Pacmanvirus) have been shown to possess an MCP with a vertical double jellyroll (DJR) fold that composes the capsid shell, along with an internal membrane bilayer.
source: All of the abovementioned viruses have been shown to possess an MCP with a vertical double jellyroll (DJR) fold that composes the capsid shell, along with an internal membrane bilayer.
evidence: Based on published structural studies.

claim: Minor capsid proteins have been identified and structurally modeled for ASFV and PBCV-1.
source: Minor capsid proteins have been identified and structurally modeled for the smaller virions ASFV and PBCV-1 (Wang et al., 2019; Shao et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: Beneath the Jyvaskylavirus capsid, the membrane vesicle follows icosahedral symmetry, although it also displays a high degree of sphericity.
source: Beneath the Jyvaskylavirus capsid, the membrane vesicle follows icosahedral symmetry, although it also displays a high degree of sphericity (Figure 5A, left).
evidence: Observed in cryo-EM reconstruction shown in Figure 5A.

claim: At the fivefold axis between the capsid and the membrane in Jyvaskylavirus, there is relatively weak density suggesting the presence of additional proteins, along with a clear bulging of the membrane vesicle at the fivefold (radius of curvature of ~275 Å).
source: At the fivefold axis between the capsid and the membrane, there is relatively weak density suggesting the presence of additional proteins (see below), along with a clear bulging of the membrane vesicle at the fivefold (radius of curvature of ~275 Å) (Figure 5A, left).
evidence: Observed in cryo-EM reconstruction.

claim: The membrane bulging at the fivefold has only been clearly observed in the closely related Melbournevirus and Tokyovirus.
source: To the best of our knowledge, this bulging has only been clearly observed in the closely related Melbournevirus and Tokyovirus.
evidence: Based on comparison with published structures.

claim: At 6.3 Å resolution alpha-helical secondary structural motifs are identifiable while the separation of β-strands became clearer beyond 5 Å.
source: At 6.3 Å resolution alpha-helical secondary structural motifs are identifiable while the separation of β-strands became clearer beyond 5 Å.
evidence: Based on general knowledge of cryo-EM resolution capabilities.

claim: The density corresponding to the Jyvaskylavirus capsomer displays unequivocally pseudo-hexameric morphology with the characteristic footprint of trimers formed by vertical DJR seen in other viruses of the kingdom Bamfordviriae.
source: Our density corresponding to the capsomer displays unequivocally pseudo-hexameric morphology with the characteristic footprint of trimers formed by vertical DJR seen in other viruses of the kingdom Bamfordviriae (Andrés et al., 2020; Ravantti et al., 2020; Simmonds et al., 2023).
evidence: Observed in cryo-EM density and supported by citations to structural studies of related viruses.

claim: AlphaFold3 predicted a model of ORF184 with a DJR fold.
source: We submitted ORF184 to AlphaFold3, which predicted a model with a DJR fold (Figure 5D; Abramson et al., 2024).
evidence: Generated using AlphaFold3 prediction software.

claim: A total of 154 copies of the MCP compose the IAU of Jyvaskylavirus.
source: The fitting of this model into density leaves no doubts about ORF184 being the MCP and a total of 154 copies of the MCP compose the IAU (Figure 5C and E).
evidence: Calculated from structural analysis.

claim: ORF142 was structurally identified as the penton protein of Jyvaskylavirus using ModelAngelo software with the HMM search procedure against the publicly available cryo-EM block-reconstructed capsid densities of Melbournevirus.
source: Then, we structurally identified the penton protein of Jyvaskylavirus as ORF142 by using the latest version of ModelAngelo software with the hidden Markov model (HMM) search procedure against the publicly available cryo-EM block-reconstructed capsid densities of the Melbournevirus, a clade A marseillevirus, at ~3.5 Å resolution (EMD-37188, 37189, 37190) (for details, see Materials and methods and Appendix 1—figure 5; Jamali et al., 2024).
evidence: Determined through cross-structural comparison using ModelAngelo software.

claim: The identification of ORF142 as penton protein was based on the hypothesis of structural conservation among conserved capsid components and partial protein sequence conservation among members of the Marseilleviridae.
source: This identification was based on the hypothesis of structural conservation among conserved capsid components and partial protein sequence conservation among members of the Marseilleviridae.
evidence: Based on comparative structural and sequence analysis.

claim: AlphaFold3 prediction of ORF142 produced a compact eight stranded β-barrel (BIDG - CHEF) typical of a jellyroll, elaborated by extended loops between strands DC and EF and a long C-terminal tail.
source: Model prediction of the ORF142 in AlphaFold3 produced a compact eight stranded β-barrel (BIDG - CHEF) typical of a jellyroll, elaborated by extended loops between strands DC and EF and a long C-terminal tail (Figure 6A, left) (Jumper et al., 2021).
evidence: Generated using AlphaFold3 prediction.

claim: ORF121 was identified as the cap protein that sits atop the pseudo-hexameric capsomers.
source: Using the same methodological strategy as for the penton protein, we identified ORF121 as this cap protein, which possesses a β-barrel fold and forms a trimer, with its N-terminal ends inserting into the crevice formed by the MCP jellyroll towers (Figure 6B).
evidence: Identified through cross-structural comparison and AlphaFold3 prediction.

claim: ORF121 possesses a β-barrel fold and forms a trimer.
source: Using the same methodological strategy as for the penton protein, we identified ORF121 as this cap protein, which possesses a β-barrel fold and forms a trimer, with its N-terminal ends inserting into the crevice formed by the MCP jellyroll towers (Figure 6B).
evidence: Determined through AlphaFold3 prediction and fitting into density.

claim: Four additional Jyvaskylavirus proteins were identified: ORF36, ORF97, ORF153, and ORF119, located beneath the pentasymmetron capsomers.
source: Using the abovementioned approach (Appendix 1—figure 5), we identified four additional Jyvaskylavirus proteins - ORF36, ORF97, ORF153, and ORF119 - located beneath the pentasymmetron capsomers.
evidence: Identified through cross-structural comparison with Melbournevirus and AlphaFold3 prediction.

claim: ORF119 was identified as the protein that runs along the edge of the trisymmetron facets, acting as a glue between adjacent capsomers belonging to two different trisymmetrons.
source: Intriguingly, ORF119 was also identified as the protein that runs along the edge of the trisymmetron facets, acting as a glue between adjacent capsomers belonging to two different trisymmetrons (Figure 7B and Appendix 1—figure 8).
evidence: Identified through structural analysis and fitting into density.

claim: The relative orientation of the ORF119 molecule beneath the pentasymmetron and along the edges of two trisymmetrons is about 90 degrees.
source: The relative orientation of the ORF119 molecule beneath the pentasymmetron and along the edges of two trisymmetrons is about 90 degrees.
evidence: Determined from structural analysis.

claim: All AlphaFold3 predicted ORFs presented unordered regions, mostly at the N- and C-terminal ends, with lengths varying depending on the protein and their location.
source: Interestingly, all AlphaFold3 predicted ORFs presented unordered regions, mostly at the N- and C-terminal ends, with lengths varying depending on the protein and their location.
evidence: Observed in AlphaFold3 predictions.

claim: When the identified Jyvaskylavirus ORF sequences were analyzed using BLASTp without restricting the search to the Melbournevirus reference, many hits were observed in other giant viruses, primarily marseillevirus.
source: However, when the identified Jyvaskylavirus ORF sequences were analyzed using BLASTp without restricting the search to the Melbournevirus reference, many hits were observed in other giant viruses, primarily marseillevirus.
evidence: Determined through BLASTp searches.

claim: Some BLASTp hits for Jyvaskylavirus ORFs scored higher than those for Melbournevirus, supporting the presence of homologous proteins in these viruses.
source: Remarkably, some of these hits scored higher than those for Melbournevirus, supporting the presence of homologous proteins in these viruses (Appendix 1—table 3).
evidence: Determined through BLASTp analysis.

claim: A distinctive feature of the internal membrane vesicle is the bulging of the lipid bilayer at the fivefold equivalent to that found in Tokyovirus.
source: Further, a distinctive feature of the internal membrane vesicle is the bulging of the lipid bilayer at the fivefold equivalent to that found in Tokyovirus (Figure 5A, left and Figure 6A; Chihara et al., 2022).
evidence: Observed in cryo-EM reconstruction and compared with published Tokyovirus structure.

claim: The identified PCs crown the membrane bulging region, and it is plausible that, along with yet unidentified proteins, they act as effectors of the bulging by tethering the membrane.
source: The identified PCs crown this region, and it is plausible that, along with yet unidentified proteins, they act as effectors of the bulging by tethering the membrane.
evidence: Inferred from structural observations and protein locations.

claim: Jyvaskylavirus is the first characterized giant virus from Finland.
source: Jyvaskylavirus is the first characterized giant virus from Finland.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The only other isolated giant viruses from the Nordic countries are the still uncharacterized Lurbovirus from Sweden and a collection of viruses capable of infecting microalgae isolated in Southern Norway.
source: So far the only other isolated giant viruses from the Nordic countries are the still uncharacterized Lurbovirus from Sweden and a collection of viruses capable of infecting microalgae isolated in Southern Norway (Kördel et al., 2021Kördel et al., 2021; Sandaa et al., 2001; Johannessen et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: There is genomic evidence of NCLDV presence in the Greenland ice sheet and of a high diversity of giant viruses, including the detection of marseilleviruses, in the Loki's Castle deep-sea vent located in the Mid-Atlantic Ridge between Iceland and Svalbard.
source: There is genomic evidence of NCLDV presence in the Greenland ice sheet and of a high diversity of giant viruses, including the detection of marseilleviruses, in the Loki's Castle deep-sea vent located in the Mid-Atlantic Ridge between Iceland and Svalbard (Perini et al., 2024; Bäckström et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to metagenomic studies.

claim: Jyvaskylavirus is the northernmost known member of the Marseilleviridae family.
source: Jyvaskylavirus belongs to clade B of the Marseilleviridae family, so far making it the northernmost known member of the family.
evidence: Based on geographic location of isolation and comparison with other known marseilleviruses.

claim: The first marseillevirus was isolated from France in 2007.
source: The first marseillevirus was isolated from France in 2007 (Boyer et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to the original marseillevirus isolation study.

claim: There are more than 60 marseillevirus isolates known, obtained from varied sample sources in seven countries over five continents.
source: Now there are more than 60 isolates known, obtained from varied sample sources in seven countries over five continents (Sahmi-Bounsiar et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to a review of marseilleviruses.

claim: The Loki's Castle marseilleviruses group together and are not close to Jyvaskylavirus, probably forming unique clusters among themselves.
source: Our genetic analysis showed that the Loki's Castle marseilleviruses group together and that they are not close to Jyvaskylavirus, probably forming unique clusters among themselves (Appendix 1—figure 3).
evidence: Determined through phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Jyvaskylavirus is the first marseillevirus found from a composting sample.
source: Jyvaskylavirus is also unique for being the first found from a composting sample, demonstrating that these giant viruses are found in water and soil samples worldwide.
evidence: Based on comparison with other marseillevirus isolation sources.

claim: The 3D reconstructed cryo-EM density at 6.3 Å resolution clearly recapitulates the architecture (T=309; ∼2500 Å vertex-to-vertex diameter) and capsid protein organization observed in Melbournevirus and Tokyovirus.
source: The 3D reconstructed cryo-EM density at 6.3 Å resolution clearly recapitulates the architecture (T=309; ∼2500 Å vertex-to-vertex diameter) and capsid protein organization observed in Melbournevirus and Tokyovirus, other members of the Marseilleviridae family (Burton-Smith et al., 2021; Chihara et al., 2022).
evidence: Based on comparison of structural features with published structures.

claim: There is structural conservation of the penton protein fold with that of other viruses such as penton proteins P31 in bacteriophage PRD1 or VP9 in archaeal virus HCIV-1 of the Bamfordviria and Helvetiavirae kingdoms.
source: There is structural conservation of the penton protein fold with that of other viruses such as penton proteins P31 in bacteriophage PRD1 or VP9 in archaeal virus HCIV-1 of the Bamfordviria and Helvetiavirae kingdoms, possessing vertical double and single jellyroll MCPs, respectively (Abrescia et al., 2004; Santos-Pérez et al., 2019).
evidence: Based on structural comparison with published structures.

claim: In ORF142, the CHEF strands are predicted to be tilted relative to the BIDG strands, with an estimated angle of approximately 60 degrees based on visual inspection.
source: However, in ORF142, the CHEF strands are predicted to be tilted relative to the BIDG strands, with an estimated angle of approximately 60 degrees based on visual inspection (Appendix 1—figure 9).
evidence: Observed in AlphaFold3 predicted model.

claim: The penton complex acts like a plug-and-play system, able to incorporate various host-recognizing vertex proteins that are interchangeable and adapt to environmental evolutionary pressures.
source: This type of penton complex acts like a plug-and-play system, able to incorporate various host-recognizing vertex proteins. These proteins are interchangeable and adapt to environmental evolutionary pressures (Gil-Carton et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous structural study.

claim: The clear presence of a network of scaffolding, cementing, and minor proteins beneath the capsid reiterates the universal requirement for the assembly of larger virus of an increased number of ancillary proteins tethering the MCPs at the vertices, within the facets and along the facets.
source: The clear presence of a network of scaffolding, cementing, and minor proteins beneath, previously observed in ASFV and Tokyovirus, but also in smaller viruses such as PBCV-1, adenovirus, and PRD1, reiterates the universal requirement for the assembly of larger virus of an increased number of ancillary proteins tethering the MCPs at the vertices, within the facets and along the facets (Abrescia et al., 2004; Burton-Smith et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2019; Chihara et al., 2022; Shao et al., 2022).
evidence: Based on structural observations and comparison with other viruses, supported by citations.

claim: ORF121 shares its fold with marseillevirus Noumeavirus NMV_189 protein (PDB ID 7QRR) (e.g. rmsd 1.5 Å, 146 Cα aligned) and virophage Zamilion vitis protein Zav19 (PDB ID 7QRJ).
source: The former four are located beneath the pentasymmetron while ORF121 is the protein capping on the top the capsomers and it shares its fold with marseillevirus Noumeavirus NMV_189 protein (PDB ID 7QRR) (e.g. rmsd 1.5 Å, 146 Cα aligned) and virophage Zamilion vitis protein Zav19 (PDB ID 7QRJ).
evidence: Determined through structural comparison with deposited structures.

claim: Two ORF119 molecules that form a homodimer are used to glue at their bases capsomers located at the edge of adjacent trisymmetrons.
source: Remarkably, two ORF119 molecules that form a homodimer are also used to glue at their bases capsomers located at the edge of adjacent trisymmetrons.
evidence: Determined from structural analysis.

claim: The orientation of the ORF119 molecule below the pentasymmetron differs from that along the edge of the trisymmetron, indicating that its binding mode depends on the structural environment.
source: The orientation of the ORF119 molecule below the pentasymmetron differs from that along the edge of the trisymmetron, indicating that its binding mode depends on the structural environment.
evidence: Inferred from structural observations.

claim: The reuse of the same protein in different regions of the facet for multiple functions highlights ORFs optimization and genetic parsimony.
source: The reuse of the same protein in different regions of the facet for multiple functions highlights ORFs optimization and genetic parsimony.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that ORF119 is used in multiple locations.

claim: ORF153 is predicted to possess about 40% of the residues unstructured.
source: One clear case is ORF153 which is predicted to possess about 40% of the residues unstructured.
evidence: Determined from AlphaFold3 prediction.

claim: The unordered regions in predicted proteins are not merely a limitation of AlphaFold3's predictive capabilities but rather reflect specific functional characteristics of these proteins, which may fold and adapt through protein partnering.
source: We propose that these regions together with flexible terminal ends are not merely a limitation of AlphaFold3's predictive capabilities but rather reflect specific functional characteristics of these proteins, which may fold and adapt through protein partnering.
evidence: Proposed interpretation of AlphaFold3 predictions.

claim: The observation that the identified Jyvaskylavirus minor capsid protein sequences are shared across other marseillaviruses supports their essential structural and stabilizing roles in these viruses.
source: Additionally, the observation that the identified Jyvaskylavirus minor capsid protein sequences are shared across other marseillaviruses supports their essential structural and stabilizing roles in these viruses.
evidence: Inferred from sequence conservation analysis.

claim: The conserved flexibility and function of intrinsically disordered proteins, despite their often-fast rate and tolerance for mutations, plays critical physiological roles across all organisms and viruses.
source: It has been shown that the conserved flexibility and function of intrinsically disordered proteins, despite their often-fast rate and tolerance for mutations, plays critical physiological roles across all organisms and viruses (Brown et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Protein P30 of the lipid-containing bacteriophage PRD1 was the first to be identified possessing a string-like structure running through adjacent virus facets, interacting with capsomers along the edges and cementing them together.
source: Protein P30 of the lipid-containing bacteriophage PRD1, structurally determined more than 20 years ago, and predicted as a disordered protein, was the first to be identified possessing a string-like structure running through adjacent virus facets, interacting with capsomers along the edges and cementing them together (Abrescia et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous structural study.

claim: Giant viruses are structurally more complex than smaller viruses, with a larger number of minor capsid proteins holding the virion together beneath the pentasymmetron and trisymmetron.
source: Giant viruses, however, are structurally more complex, with a larger number of minor capsid proteins holding the virion together beneath the pentasymmetron and trisymmetron.
evidence: Inferred from structural observations and comparison with smaller viruses.

claim: Deciphering the atomic interactions and specific roles of minor capsid proteins in particle assembly will require higher resolution for the different components.
source: While our current study advances our understanding of this complexity by identifying various ORFs and positioning their models in the density map, deciphering their atomic interactions and specific roles in particle assembly will require higher resolution for the different components.
evidence: Acknowledged limitation of current study and future direction.

claim: Marseillevirus DNA polymerase sequences are present in metagenomes from Finnish drinking water distribution systems.
source: Marseillevirus DNA polymerase sequences are present in metagenomes from Finnish drinking water distribution systems (Tiwari et al., 2021) hinting to a wide distribution of these viruses and still unknown ecological role in Central and Eastern Finland.
evidence: Supported by citation to metagenomic study.

claim: Electron microscopy analyses revealed high structural diversity of giant viruses and virus-like particles in soil, suggesting a gap in knowledge in the diversity and ecology of environmental virus-host interactions.
source: In addition, electron microscopy analyses revealed high structural diversity of giant viruses and virus-like particles in soil, suggesting a gap in knowledge in the diversity and ecology of environmental virus-host interactions (Hylling et al., 2020; Fischer et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Broader sampling and new isolation attempts are essential to determine the distribution of giant viruses.
source: Despite the technical challenges that prevented us from characterizing all isolated viruses in this study, our findings underscore the importance that broader sampling and new isolation attempts are essential to determine the distribution of these viruses.
evidence: Inferred from the findings and limitations of the current study.

claim: The use of host species isolated locally might avoid isolation bias toward the reference strains, giving a better idea of viral diversity and allowing the description of unique viral groups.
source: The use of host species isolated locally might avoid isolation bias toward the reference strains, giving a better idea of viral diversity and allowing the description of unique viral groups.
evidence: Proposed methodological consideration based on study experience.

claim: Marseilleviruses found in diverse locations and environments worldwide show a strictly conserved architecture, using equivalent pseudo-hexameric building blocks and a plethora of ancillary proteins.
source: In summary, marseilleviruses found in diverse locations and environments worldwide show a strictly conserved architecture, using equivalent pseudo-hexameric building blocks and a plethora of ancillary proteins.
evidence: Concluded from structural analysis and comparison with other marseilleviruses.

claim: The adaptation of marseilleviruses relies on the number, fold, and length of disordered regions in the minor capsid proteins, as well as the membrane composition, which not only facilitate correct assembly but would also modulate the structural stability of the virus across various environments.
source: We suggest that this adaptation relies on the number, fold, and length of disordered regions in the minor capsid proteins, as well as the membrane composition. These factors not only facilitate correct assembly but would also modulate the structural stability of the virus across various environments.
evidence: Proposed hypothesis based on structural observations.

claim: Of the 96 environmental samples tested, 10 had viral presence confirmed by the appearance of cytopathic effect in cultures of A. castellanii followed by visualization of negative stained viral-like particles by electron microscopy (10.41% isolation success in A. castellanii).
source: Of these samples, 10 had viral presence confirmed by the appearance of cytopathic effect (CPE) in cultures of A. castellanii followed by visualization of negative stained viral-like particles by electron microscopy (10.41% isolation success in A. castellanii).
evidence: Reported from isolation experiments.

claim: Adjusting for sample type and unique viral morphologies found, 53 unique sample types were tested and three distinct viral morphologies were found (5.66% isolation success in A. castellanii).
source: Adjusting for sample type and unique viral morphologies found, we have then tested 53 unique sample types and found three distinct viral morphologies (5.66% isolation success in A. castellanii) (see Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Calculated from isolation experiment results.

claim: Some CPE-positive samples contained mixed viral populations.
source: Some of the CPE-positive samples contained mixed viral populations.
evidence: Observed during isolation experiments.

claim: Samples collected from experimental aquaria had a mixture of three different viral morphotypes with dimensions ranging from approximately 200 to 300 nm side-to-side.
source: Samples collected from experimental aquaria had a mixture of three different viral morphotypes with dimensions ranging from approximately 200 to 300 nm side-to-side, highlighting a previously unexplored diversity of giant viruses in this setting (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: Observed in electron microscopy images shown in Figure 1A-C.

claim: One sample from a recirculating aquaculture tank possessed the diamond-shaped and loose-capsid morphologies seen in the aquaria samples.
source: One sample from a recirculating aquaculture tank also possessed the diamond-shaped and loose-capsid morphologies seen in the aquaria samples.
evidence: Observed in electron microscopy.

claim: The high amount of nutrients in the fish aquaria or tanks might have enriched for protozoa and thus favored giant virus isolation.
source: The high amount of nutrients in the fish aquaria or tanks might have enriched for protozoa and thus favored our giant virus isolation, in a pattern similar to the original methodology for isolating giant viruses (Arslan et al., 2011).
evidence: Proposed explanation for isolation success, supported by citation to original giant virus isolation methodology.

claim: The isolate from sample 85 had a single morphotype of approximately 200 nm in size, displaying an icosahedral shape with particles that were mostly genome-filled and a few that were empty.
source: The isolate from sample 85 had a single morphotype of approximately 200 nm in size, displaying an icosahedral shape with particles that were mostly genome-filled and a few that were empty (Figure 1D).
evidence: Observed in electron microscopy shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The empty particles of Jyvaskylavirus possibly displayed an internal membrane beneath the capsid.
source: The empty particles possibly displayed an internal membrane beneath the capsid (Figure 1D, center).
evidence: Observed in electron microscopy image shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Sample 85 was collected from the municipal Waste Treatment Centre, Jyväskylä, Finland.
source: This sample was collected from the municipal Waste Treatment Centre, Jyväskylä, Finland.
evidence: Stated in the manuscript.

claim: Sample 85 was in soil state and originated from a mixture of 70% garden waste, 15% woodchips, and 15% pretreated biowaste.
source: The sample was in soil state and originated from a mixture of 70% garden waste, 15% woodchips, and 15% pretreated biowaste.
evidence: Stated in the manuscript.

claim: Jyvaskylavirus has a fast replication cycle in its A. castellanii host.
source: Jyvaskylavirus has a fast replication cycle in its A. castellanii host, only causes CPE in A. polyphaga or V. vermiformis in high concentrations likely due to cytotoxic effect of the virus preparation, is sensitive to chloroform treatment (10% for 10 min), and is stable for long periods (up to 109 days) even at 37°C (Appendix 1 and Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: Determined from growth curve experiments.

claim: Jyvaskylavirus only causes CPE in A. polyphaga or V. vermiformis in high concentrations likely due to cytotoxic effect of the virus preparation.
source: Jyvaskylavirus has a fast replication cycle in its A. castellanii host, only causes CPE in A. polyphaga or V. vermiformis in high concentrations likely due to cytotoxic effect of the virus preparation, is sensitive to chloroform treatment (10% for 10 min), and is stable for long periods (up to 109 days) even at 37°C (Appendix 1 and Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: Observed in host range experiments.

claim: Jyvaskylavirus is sensitive to chloroform treatment (10% for 10 min).
source: Jyvaskylavirus has a fast replication cycle in its A. castellanii host, only causes CPE in A. polyphaga or V. vermiformis in high concentrations likely due to cytotoxic effect of the virus preparation, is sensitive to chloroform treatment (10% for 10 min), and is stable for long periods (up to 109 days) even at 37°C (Appendix 1 and Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: Determined from chloroform sensitivity assay.

claim: Jyvaskylavirus is stable for long periods (up to 109 days) even at 37°C.
source: Jyvaskylavirus has a fast replication cycle in its A. castellanii host, only causes CPE in A. polyphaga or V. vermiformis in high concentrations likely due to cytotoxic effect of the virus preparation, is sensitive to chloroform treatment (10% for 10 min), and is stable for long periods (up to 109 days) even at 37°C (Appendix 1 and Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: Determined from stability assay.

claim: A fast replication cycle is a feature also shown for other marseilleviruses.
source: A fast replication cycle is a feature also shown for other marseilleviruses (Boyer et al., 2009; Fabre et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on marseilleviruses.

claim: Membrane-related structures located near or nearly attached to the luminal side of the large vesicle are discernible in infected cells.
source: Membrane-related structures located near or nearly attached to the luminal side of the large vesicle are discernible (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: Observed in TEM images shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: Membrane-derived assembled structures might serve during virus morphogenesis.
source: These membrane-derived assembled structures might serve during virus morphogenesis (Figure 4D).
evidence: Inferred from TEM observations.

claim: A putative assembly path can be extrapolated from the analysis of images of particles, which transition from a half-assembled icosahedron to a particle with an open vertex through the orderly accumulation of capsid proteins.
source: A putative assembly path can be extrapolated from the analysis of images of particles, which transition from a half-assembled icosahedron to a particle with an open vertex through the orderly accumulation of capsid proteins (Figure 4F).
evidence: Inferred from TEM images showing different stages of particle formation.

claim: The open vertex in assembling Jyvaskylavirus particles is potentially used for genome packaging, and it is subsequently closed by the plugging of peripentonal and penton proteins.
source: This open vertex is potentially used for genome packaging, and it is subsequently closed by the plugging of peripentonal and penton proteins.
evidence: Inferred from structural observations and knowledge of virus assembly.

claim: Jyvaskylavirus virion possesses a diameter of 2516 Å (vertex-to-vertex).
source: Jyvaskylavirus icosahedral virion, determined to 6.3 Å resolution as judged by the gold-standard Fourier shell correlation, possesses a diameter of 2516 Å (vertex-to-vertex) and a triangulation number T=309 (h=7, k=13) (Figure 5A, Appendix 1—figure 4, and Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: Measured from cryo-EM reconstruction.

claim: 3742 useful particles were obtained from 17,720 movies for Jyvaskylavirus cryo-EM reconstruction.
source: After four data collections we obtained 3742 useful particles from 17,720 movies.
evidence: Reported from cryo-EM data processing.

claim: Ewald sphere correction was applied to the final Jyvaskylavirus cryo-EM map, resulting in a resolution of 6.3 Å and a notable improvement in the map interpretability and FSC curve.
source: Finally, Ewald sphere correction was applied to the final map, resulting in a resolution of 6.3 Å and a notable improvement in the map interpretability and FSC curve (Appendix 1—figure 4).
evidence: Reported from cryo-EM data processing.

claim: The best-ranked AlphaFold3 predicted model of ORF184 had a confidence level of 95% based on the predicted local-distance difference test.
source: The best-ranked predicted model had a confidence level of 95% based on the predicted local-distance difference test, which ranged from 28.7% to 98.9% across the residues.
evidence: Reported from AlphaFold3 prediction output.

claim: The MCP model was rigid body refined into the 6.3 Å resolution map using PHENIX real-space refinement leading to a CCmask of 52%.
source: The three molecules were rigid body refined into the 6.3 Å resolution map using PHENIX real-space refinement (Afonine et al., 2018) leading to a CCmask of 52%.
evidence: Reported from structural refinement.

claim: The pentameric assembly model of Melbournevirus was refined using rigid-body refinement in PHENIX, yielding a CCmask of 57.3%.
source: To assess the metric of this fitting (Appendix 1—figure 7), the 3.5 Å fivefold Melbournevirus block 3D density (EMDB-37190) was boxed around the pentameric assembly model and refined as a whole using rigid-body refinement in PHENIX, yielding a CCmask of 57.3%.
evidence: Reported from structural refinement.

claim: The same pentameric model fitted into the 6.3 Å Jyvaskylavirus 3D cryo-EM density resulted in a CCmask of 33%, consistent with the limited resolution of the capsid map and below regions.
source: The same pentameric model was subsequently fitted into the 6.3 Å Jyvaskylavirus 3D cryo-EM density (previously boxed around the model), resulting in a lower CCmask of 33%, consistent with the limited resolution of the capsid map and below regions.
evidence: Reported from structural fitting analysis.
